title: Bodybuilding is killing me (Hypertrophy Log #8)
summary: Training log of an upper day (weighted ring decline push-ups, ring rollouts, cross-bench pullovers, pronated preacher curls, strapped rear-delt rows) and a lower day (heels-elevated SSB squat, Zercher and SSB good mornings, neck). He then explains his template-based training, his move to 5 days a week for recovery, and announces weekly Saturday streams.
claims: Ring decline push-ups hit the whole chest, especially the upper chest, and give more range of motion than floor push-ups; go down until the rings reach the armpits for a big pec stretch
Load push-ups with a sturdy backpack that sits tight on the shoulders; he uses 70 lb in a 200-lb-capacity pack and warns against flimsy ones
Safe movements you can bail out of, like push-ups, can be done in low rep ranges at high intensity
The value of a hard contraction is mostly that it helps you feel the target muscle, which makes the stretch more effective
Start ring rollouts with a partial range to build shoulder mobility and core resilience
At 220 lb and high body fat he still has a full six-pack only because he trains abs; 2-3 ab exercises a week, about 3 sets, is plenty
Pullovers will transform your physique; he uses about 95 lb, a slow controlled negative and a range where the dumbbell nearly reaches the floor
Do pullovers across the bench with the hips lower than the shoulders, so the body curves like a banana and the rib cage, serratus and lats get a bigger stretch
Pullovers are an underrated core movement and build rib-cage, serratus, oblique and ab definition even at high body fat; he does them every week
He trains in giant sets of three exercises, 3 sets each
Pronated preacher curls emphasise the brachioradialis for thick forearms; use a slow tempo and don't let the shoulders roll forward
Rest-pause on isolation lifts: resting 3-15 seconds at the top earns an extra very high-intensity rep
Grinding a hard rep is a skill you learn separately for each exercise; it does not carry over automatically
Ab isolation is non-negotiable for a bodybuilder
For rear-delt rows, loop the handle around the wrist like a strap rather than gripping it, and focus on driving the elbow up and back
Body English is fine on heavy back rows like Yates rows but not on rear-delt isolation
Flaring the elbow to 90 degrees targets rear delts but hurts his shoulders, so he uses an in-between angle; no lift is worth shoulder discomfort
After several serious knee injuries he warms up with bodyweight squats and then goblet squats on a slant, before heavy squats
Squatting with the heels elevated keeps the torso upright, spares the lower back and puts more emphasis on the quads
Goblet squats would be an ideal quad builder if they could be loaded to 200-300 lb, but 140 lb for 20 reps is not a challenge for him
With flat feet the safety squat bar tips you forward onto the posterior chain; with the heels elevated, push the handles up rather than pulling them down to stay vertical
Never dive-bomb squats; a slow, controlled descent is safer and gives the quads more stimulus
He works up 135, 200, 250, 300+ lb and stops 2 reps short of failure on SSB squats without safeties
His leg day is one quad movement and one hip hinge or knee flexion, 3 sets each; trained really hard, that is enough
He dropped Zercher good mornings because holding the bar, not the posterior chain, became the limiting factor
Training your weak link only makes sense if that quality serves your goal; a strongman needs a strong Zercher hold, a bodybuilder does not
He trains the back of the neck every lower day, with a controlled negative and an explosive concentric
He now has a template instead of a program: upper or lower days filled from a memorised list of exercises with known weights and rep ranges
Advanced lifters should refuse to do exercises they dislike; there are enough options to always pick ones you look forward to
Try new exercises, but drop any that don't work for you
Novices and early intermediates should not train by template, because they end up winging it and building an unbalanced physique
He went from 7 to 6 to 5 training days a week: three upper days (two chest/back, one arms) and two lower days
Hard leg sessions now need 72 hours or more to recover; soreness from heavy RDLs peaks around 48 hours, so lower body three times a week is too much
Training less often lets him train harder, and his gains and rate of progress are unchanged
Optimal recovery is simple: less frequency, less junk volume, better nutrition and lots of passive rest such as reading on the couch
You cannot wait for life's difficulties to stop; you have to get things done in the storm
To avoid losing weight and strength on flights, eat greasy airport food and drink hydration packets during the flight
